etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English boy.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Clipping of ベルボーイ (berubōi), borrowed from English bellboy.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From English massage, from French massage, from masser (“to massage”), borrowed around the end of the 18th century from Arabic مَسَّ (massa, “feel, touch”) + French -age.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English rocket.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English locket.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 一言 (MC ʔjit ngjon, literally “one + speech, word”). The goon, so likely the initial borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift in pronunciation from ichigon above, using the kan'on of gen for the 言 character.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 一(ひと) (hito, “one”) + 言(こと) (koto, “word, speech”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift in reading from 万(ばん)歳(ぜい) (banzei) below, keeping the older goon reading for the second character and adopting the relatively newer kan'on reading for the first character. Doublet of マンセー (mansē).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 萬歲 (MC mjonH sjwejH). The kan'on, so likely a later borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 萬歲 (MC mjonH sjwejH). The goon, so likely the initial borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 上(あ)がり (agari, “rising, going up”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 上(あ)がる (agaru, “to rise, to go up”)) + 下(お)り (ori, “descending, going down”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 下(お)りる (oriru, “to descend, to go down”)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 上(あ)がり (agari, “rising, going up”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 上(あ)がる (agaru, “to rise, to go up”)) + 下(さ)がり (sagari, “coming down, hanging down”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 下(さ)がる (sagaru, “to come down, to hang down”)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 上(あ)げ (age, “raising, lifting up”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 上(あ)げる (ageru, “to raise, lift”)) + 下(お)ろし (oroshi, “lowering, bringing down”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 下(お)ろす (orosu, “to lower, bring down”)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 上(あ)げ (age, “raising, lifting”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 上(あ)げる (ageru, “to raise, lift”)) + 下(く)だし (kudashi, “putting something down; passing something through one's gut”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 下(くだ)す (kudasu, “to put something down; to pass something through one's gut”)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 上(あ)げ (age, “raising, lifting”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 上(あ)げる (ageru, “to raise, lift”)) + 下(さ)げ (sage, “lowering something, hanging something down”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 下(さ)げる (sageru, “to lower something, to hang something down”)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 上(うえ) (ue, “up”) + 下(した) (shita, “down”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 上(かみ) (kami, “up, upper; first”) + 下(しも) (shimo, “down, lower; last”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 上(か)り (kari, “rising in tone”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 上(か)る (karu, “to rise in tone”)) + 下(め)り (meri, “falling in tone”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 下(め)る (meru, “to fall in tone”)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ɕauka/ → /ɕɔːka/ → /ɕoːka/
From Middle Chinese compound 上下 (dzyangᴴ hæ^X, literally “up and down”). Compare modern Cantonese reading soeng⁶ haa⁶ or Hakka song-ha.
The kan'on, so likely a later borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/d͡ʑauka/ → /d͡ʑɔːka/ → /d͡ʑoːka/
From Middle Chinese compound 上下 (dzyangᴴ hæ^X, literally “up and down”). Compare modern Min Nan alternative reading chiūⁿ hā.
A mixed reading, using the goon of jō and the kan'on of ka.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/d͡ʑauɡe/ → /d͡ʑɔːɡe/ → /d͡ʑoːɡe/
From Middle Chinese compound 上下 (dzyangᴴ hæ^X, literally “up and down”). Compare modern Cantonese reading soeng⁶ haa⁶, Hakka song-ha, or Min Nan alternative reading chiūⁿ hā.
The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 上(の)ぼり (nobori, “climbing, going up”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 上(のぼ)る (noboru, “to climb, to go up”)) + 下(お)り (ori, “descending, going down”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 下(お)りる (oriru, “to descend, to go down”)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 上(の)ぼり (nobori, “climbing, going up”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 上(のぼ)る (noboru, “to climb, to go up”)) + 下(くだ)り (kudari, “descending, coming down”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 下(くだ)る (kudaru, “to descend a path, to come down a path”)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 不足 (MC pjuw tsjowk, “not + enough”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 世界 (MC syejH keajH), originally a translation of Sanskrit लोकधातु (lokadhātu, “region or part of the world”). Compare Hokkien 世界 (sè-kài).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 元氣 (MC ngjwon khj+jH, literally “first, fundamental, source + vapor, spirit, energy”). In Chinese cosmology, this represented the fundamental force that permeates all matter and life. Early Japanese borrowed this word and meaning. Later, this spelling was conflated with the meaning of homophone 減気 (genki, “recovery from illness”), adding in the modern senses related to healthy and wellness.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 元(もと) (moto, “origin, beginning”) + 気(き) (ki, “sense; mood; energy; spirit”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Analyzed by references as either a compound of 再来 (sarai, “two next, the one after next”) + 月 (getsu, “month”), or as a compound of 再 (sa, “again, one more”) + 来月 (raigetsu, “next month”).
First attested in 1799.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Derived from 名 (na, “name”) + 前 (mae, front). Compare the semantics of Latin praenomen.
Appears as a term only in the last few centuries, becoming more widely used during the Meiji period.
Similarity to English name and other Indo-European words derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ is coincidental.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 夜(よ) (yo, “night”) + 中(なか) (naka, “middle”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Apparently from Middle Chinese 夜中 (MC yaeH trjuwng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 夜(よ) (yo, “night”) + 中(ちゅう) (-chū, “during, throughout”, rendaku form 中(じゅう) (jū)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 安心 (MC 'an sim). Compare modern Chinese 安心 (ānxīn).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Ultimately from Middle Chinese compound 安心 (MC 'an sim), likely through 安(あん)心(しん) (anshin) above. The shin changes to jin as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of Old Japanese elements 手 (te, “hand”) + 前 (mae, “front”), originally meaning “that which is just in front of one's hand”.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Corruption of temae. The vowel shift emphasizes the confrontational sense of the term. This flattening of diphthongs to monophthongs is characteristic of Tokyo's Shitamachi dialect. Compare おめえ (omē, from お前 (omae)), ねえ (nē, from ない), やべえ (yabē, from やばい (yabai)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From 振(ふ)り (furi, “assigning”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 振(ふ)る (furu, “to assign, to stick on, to apportion”)) + 仮名(かな) (kana, “kana”).
The kana changes to gana as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
First attested in 1813.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/isi/ → /isɨ/ → /isu/
Originally 倚子 (ishi), referring to seats with or without rests used by higher court officials. With the arrival of Zen Buddhism to Japan, possibly a later borrowing from Middle Chinese 椅子 (MC 'jeX tsiX) or directly from Mandarin 椅子 (yǐzi, literally "chair" + diminutive suffix), the meaning shifted to wooden seats used by priests.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Seems to be a Japanese coinage from Middle Chinese-derived roots, as a compound of 残 (zan, “remaining, lingering”) + 念 (nen, “concern”). Appears in texts from the late 1500s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From さすがに (sasuga ni) with omission of the final に (ni). The standalone term without the final に (ni) is first cited to the late 800s.
The kanji are jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 火 (ka, “fire”) + 口 (kō, “hole”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 火 (hi, “fire”) + 口 (kuchi, “hole”). The kuchi changes to guchi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 火(ほ) (ho-, 被(ひ)覆(ふく)形(けい) (hifukukei, “bound form”) of 火(ひ) (hi, “fire”)) + 口(くち) (kuchi, “hole; mouth”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 片 (kata, “part”) + 仮名 (kana). 片 is in turn a cognate with 方 (kata).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨kidi⟩ → /kiʑi/
Compound of 生 (ki, “crude, pure, raw”) + 地 (ji, “earth; skin”).
Originally written 木地, a transparent compound of 木 (ki, “wood”) + 地 (di, “earth; skin”), referring to the bare wooden surface of an object before lacquer or paint was applied.
Attested from at least the medieval period in this sense. (First cited in Vocabulario da Lingoa de Iapam)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Appears to be from Middle Chinese 石鹼 (MC dzyek keamX, literally “stone + lye; soap”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 積極(せっきょく) (sekkyoku, “positive procession towards an objective; the positive pole”) + 的(てき) (-teki, adjective-forming suffix).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Unknown, but thought to be related to English civil clothes, Savile Row, or Cheviot.
The kanji are ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)); they literally mean "back" + "wide" ("wide-backed").

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 誕生(たんじょう) (tanjō, “birth”) + 日(び) (-bi, “day”).
The hi reading for 日 changes to bi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 誕生(たんじょう) (tanjō, “birth”) + 日(にち) (-nichi, counter for day of a month).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Compound of 道 (chi, “road, way”) + 交う (kau, “cross, exchange”). The kau changes to gau as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
First cited to the Kagerō Nikki of 974, and likely extant earlier given the initial citing in 965 of derived form 違える (chigaeru, “to keep something from happening”)
Similar, but not related, to tagau reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Compound of 手 (ta, “hand”, bound form) + 交う (kau, “cross, exchange”). The kau changes to gau as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
First cited to the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The kanji are ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Appears to be a coinage in Japanese from Middle Chinese-derived roots, as a compound of 風 (fū, “wind”) + 船 (sen, “ship, boat, vessel”).
First cited to a text from 1860.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Probably originally a transcription of Sanskrit मोह (moha, “folly”), used as a cant term among monks. However, Sanskrit पाक (pāka, “naïve, foolish”) is more similar phonetically and grammatically.
Alternatively, may have arisen from the same root as Old Japanese 痴 (woko, modern oko, “stupidity, ridiculousness”). However, this theory is problematic phonologically, as the /b/ ↔ /w/ shift is difficult to explain.
The characters 馬鹿 (literally “horse + deer”) are ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)), probably chosen as an allusion to Literary Chinese 指鹿為馬 (“to deliberately misinterpret and invert right and wrong”, literally “to point to a deer and call it a horse”) (see that entry for more).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the 未然形 (mizenkei, irrealis stem) of 騒ぐ (sawagu, “to make noise”) + しい (shii, “adjectivizing suffix”).
